summary: This document specifies use of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection in RBridge campuses, based on the RBridge Channel extension to TRILL. BFD is a widely deployed OAM mechanism in IP and MPLS networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7175 defines how TRILL RBridges carry Bidirectional Forwarding Detection messages. These checks can reveal a data-plane failure sooner than waiting for a missing TRILL Hello, including failures that affect unicast traffic only.

questions: how does trill detect neighbor failure
subtitle: How TRILL RBridges use Bidirectional Forwarding Detection to check data-plane connectivity.

tldr.problem: TRILL Hello messages can take a long time to reveal a failed neighbor and cannot detect some failures that affect unicast traffic but not multicast.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7175 carries BFD Control and optional Echo messages in unicast RBridge Channel frames, with hop-count checks and authentication options.
tldr.outcome: The extension provides a continuity check for the TRILL data plane. RFC 7175 was updated by RFC 8564.

today: RFC 7175 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014. It has been updated by RFC 8564.

sections.title: Why TRILL Needs a Fast Continuity Check
sections.content:
TRILL uses IS-IS Hello messages to check neighbor connectivity, but failure detection depends on a Holding Time commonly set to tens of seconds and cannot be expressed below one second. Some failures affect unicast frames while multicast Hellos still pass, so the Hello check will not detect them.

Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is a low-overhead method for rapid connectivity-failure detection. RFC 7175 defines how BFD packets are encapsulated over TRILL using the RBridge Channel.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL Hellos may take too long to detect a failure, and they do not test unicast forwarding. BFD sends checks that test whether the TRILL data path works between neighbors.

sections.title: BFD Sessions over the RBridge Channel
sections.content:
TRILL supports one-hop and multi-hop BFD Control sessions, plus optional one-hop BFD Echo. Asynchronous and demand modes must be supported. There is at most one Control session from one RBridge to another for each local TRILL port, and both sides take the Active role by sending initial packets.

TRILL BFD checks the TRILL data plane above the link technology. Link-layer OAM is separate and outside this RFC's scope. If a link aggregation appears as one logical interface, only one TRILL BFD session can be established over it.
sections.plainLanguage: A BFD Control session is tied to a TRILL port, and both neighbors begin by sending. The session checks TRILL forwarding rather than the lower-level link technology.

sections.title: Control Frames and Hop Checks
sections.content:
BFD Control messages use unicast RBridge Channel frames. One-hop frames used for rapid failure detection should receive high transmission priority. A router sends them only after IS-IS confirms bidirectional connectivity and both neighbors advertise that BFD is enabled.

Before normal BFD processing, a receiver checks the TRILL header. It discards frames with a nonzero multi-destination bit. For one-hop sessions the received hop count must be 0x3F, or 0x3E if already decremented. For multi-hop sessions it must not be below a configurable threshold that defaults to 0x30.
sections.plainLanguage: Control checks use unicast frames and begin only after both routers confirm the adjacency. The receiver checks the frame's hop count and discards values that do not fit the session.

sections.title: Echo Frames
sections.content:
A BFD Echo frame is sent to a neighbor and forwarded back through normal TRILL data forwarding. The originating RBridge uses the returned frame to test the path. Some loop-suppression behavior prevents a router from returning the frame, so those routers cannot support Echo.

Echo should be sent only when a Control session is established, the neighbor advertises Echo support, the adjacency is in Report state and the originator wants to use the optional feature. Returned frames must have the expected hop count and multi-hop flag; a nonzero multi-destination bit requires discard.
sections.plainLanguage: An Echo frame goes to a neighbor and returns through normal TRILL forwarding. The sender checks the returned frame's header before counting it as a successful test.

sections.title: Default Authentication
sections.content:
If IS-IS authentication is not active between neighbors, TRILL BFD is unsecured by default. If IS-IS authentication is active, BFD Control frames must by default use Meticulous Keyed SHA1 authentication with keys derived from the shared IS-IS secret.

The key derivation includes the originating port ID and system ID. Other keys or security modes may be configured. The RFC leaves Echo authentication to the implementation because the originator checks the returned frame.
sections.plainLanguage: By default, BFD Control uses the neighbors' shared IS-IS secret when IS-IS authentication is active. Without IS-IS authentication, BFD is unsecured unless configured otherwise.

sections.title: Security and Assigned Channel Numbers
sections.content:
BFD authentication can authenticate message payloads, but BFD over TRILL does not provide encryption. The hop-count and multi-destination checks address spoofing and denial-of-service concerns described in the RFC. General security guidance also appears in the referenced BFD, RBridge Channel and TRILL specifications.

IANA assigned RBridge Channel protocol number 0x002 for BFD Control and 0x003 for BFD Echo.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication can verify BFD messages but does not hide them. The RFC assigns separate channel numbers to Control and Echo traffic.
